common_name: Duchess of Oldenburg Apple (Cold-Hardy Russian Cooking Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 3-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Duchess of Oldenburg is a Russian heirloom apple brought to the United States in the 1830s and 40s, valued from the start for extreme cold hardiness that let orchardists in the harshest northern climates grow quality apples for the first time, and it became an important parent in the breeding of many later cold-hardy varieties. The medium-sized fruit has red-striped skin over a yellow background, and the crisp, juicy, notably tart flesh is prized above all for cooking, making exceptionally flavorful applesauce and pies, though it can be eaten fresh by those who enjoy a sharply tart apple. Fruit ripens in mid to late summer, earlier than most storage apples, and does not keep long, so plan to use or process it within a few weeks of harvest.

common_name: Tolman Sweet Apple (Classic New England Sweet Baking Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; very cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 3-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Tolman Sweet is a New England heirloom dating to the early 1800s, one of the classic old-fashioned 'sweet apple' varieties once grown widely across colonial and early American orchards specifically for their low-acid, honeyed sweetness, distinct from the tart-sweet balance of most familiar modern apples. The pale yellow-green skin, sometimes lightly blushed with red near the stem, covers firm, dry, mild, sugary flesh that is exceptional baked whole, since the sweetness needs no added sugar, and it was also historically valued as a good keeper and a favorite for livestock feed and cider blending. The tree is notably cold-hardy and dependable, and while sweet apples have fallen out of fashion compared with tart-sweet modern varieties, Tolman Sweet remains a worthwhile piece of American orchard history for gardeners interested in historic baking apples.

common_name: Black Oxford Apple (Maine Heirloom Long-Keeping Purple-Black Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy and best adapted to zones 3-7, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Black Oxford originated in Paris, Maine in the 1790s and takes its name from its remarkably dark skin — deep purple, nearly black, and covered with a dusty blue-gray bloom — one of the most visually striking apples in American horticulture. Fresh off the tree in fall the dense, firm flesh is sharply tart, but Black Oxford is famous for its extraordinary keeping ability, mellowing and sweetening in cold storage over months and often holding excellent quality clear into spring, longer than almost any other apple variety. This long storage life made it historically valuable in northern New England before mechanical refrigeration, and it remains prized today by cider makers and heirloom orchardists both for its keeping quality and its distinctive appearance. Harvest in mid to late fall and store cool for the best results, tasting periodically since the flavor genuinely improves with age.

common_name: Melrose Apple (Ohio State Apple, Jonathan x Delicious Cross)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Melrose requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Melrose was bred by Ohio State University and the USDA from a cross of Jonathan and Red Delicious, released in 1944 and later named the official state apple of Ohio, developed with the specific goal of combining Jonathan's rich flavor with Red Delicious's storage life and size. The large, firm fruit has red-striped skin over a green-yellow background, and the crisp, dense flesh offers a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well both fresh and in the kitchen, equally good for eating out of hand, baking, and sauce. Melrose stores notably well for a mid-century American apple, often keeping several months in good cold storage, and the vigorous, productive tree has made it a lasting favorite for Midwestern home orchards even as many contemporary releases have faded from popularity.

common_name: Gravenstein Apple (Historic Early-Season Sauce and Baking Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gravenstein is a triploid variety that needs two different compatible pollinizer varieties nearby (its own pollen is not viable) and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, ensuring two different compatible pollinizer varieties are planted nearby, since Gravenstein is a triploid and cannot pollinize itself or other trees. Gravenstein traces to northern Europe in the 1600s and became world-famous after its introduction to Sonoma County, California in the 1820s, where the region's climate proved so ideal that Gravenstein orchards once dominated the local economy and gave the apple lasting fame as a California heritage crop. The fruit ripens unusually early, in mid to late summer well ahead of most storage apples, with crisp, juicy, aromatic flesh balancing bright tartness and real sweetness that is outstanding for fresh eating, and especially prized for applesauce and baking, where its flavor is considered exceptional. Gravenstein is not a long keeper and bruises easily, so it is best picked and used promptly rather than stored, which is part of why it remains more popular with home gardeners and local markets than large-scale commercial shipping operations.
